title: King Vasabha
biography: Vasabha (67–111 CE) stands as a pivotal hydraulic innovator, credited with constructing eleven major reservoirs (tanks) that expanded Anuradhapura's irrigable acreage significantly. His lengthy 44-year reign enabled systemic agrarian intensification: improved water distribution, higher rice yields, and stronger revenue flows. He also sponsored numerous temples, embedding his legitimacy within both material prosperity and Buddhist merit-making. Vasabha's engineering legacy influenced subsequent kings' emphasis on tank construction as royal duty.

title: King Jayavira Bandara
biography: Jayavira Bandara ruled Kandy for 41 years during the Portuguese conquest of the lowlands. He maintained highland independence and harbored the Tooth Relic, preserving Buddhist legitimacy. His reign secured Kandy as the last bastion of Sinhalese kingship against colonial encroachment.

title: King Darubhatika Tissa
biography: Darubhatika Tissa (47 BCE) followed Vatuka within the same year, signaling unresolved contention. His reign’s brevity precluded distinctive royal projects. Chronic preservation of his name serves as evidence of persistent dynastic recording practices even amidst rapid claimant cycling.

title: Emperor Constantine I the Great
biography: Transformative emperor who legalized Christianity across the empire via the Edict of Milan (313 CE), convened the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE), and founded the new imperial capital of Constantinople.
internationalConnections: Shifted the geopolitical center of the Greco-Roman world to the Bosporus, bridging Europe and Asia.

title: King Alagakkonara
biography: Alagakkonara ruled Jaffna for nine years, navigating pressures from Gampola and the emerging Kotte kingdom. He maintained Hindu institutions and coastal trade, though his reign witnessed growing political competition from southern powers seeking to curb Jaffna's autonomy.

title: King Ezana of Aksum
biography: King of Aksum who adopted Christianity for the empire around 330 CE, minted gold coins bearing the Christian cross, and expanded trade networks across the Red Sea and Nile valley.
